title: Segmentation of sparse coronary artery calcifications in computed tomography via 2.5D multi-slice feature fusion
content:
by Sun-Woo Pi, Jun-Hyeon Sim, Byoung-Dai Lee

Objective

Accurate segmentation of coronary artery calcification (CAC) on computed tomography (CT) is critical for reliable cardiovascular risk assessment but remains challenging due to the small and sparse nature of calcified lesions. Although 3D models improve inter-slice consistency, their computational and memory demands motivate alternatives for high-resolution CT segmentation. This study investigates whether the essential inter-slice continuity required for CAC segmentation can be recovered using a reusable 2.5D design compatible with standard 2D networks.

Methods

We propose a 2.5D segmentation framework that augments conventional 2D encoder–decoder architectures with a localized multi-slice feature fusion module. The framework selectively restores inter-slice continuity by refining a reference slice through self-attention and incorporating anatomically aligned context from its immediate neighboring slices via cross-attention, without volumetric processing. The module is encoder-agnostic and plug-and-play, enabling seamless integration into both convolutional and Transformer-based backbones. The approach was evaluated using patient-level five-fold cross-validation on a public CAC dataset comprising 433 cardiac-gated CT scans with vessel-wise annotations.

Results

Across all evaluated backbones, the proposed framework consistently improved mean Dice Similarity Coefficient and mean Intersection over Union relative to paired 2D baselines, with additional parameters and computation. The largest class-wise gains were observed in underrepresented artery categories. Attention map analysis provided qualitative support for anatomically coherent inter-slice aggregation. Comparisons with the evaluated 3D models showed competitive segmentation performance with shorter inference times and generally lower peak GPU memory.

Conclusion

This study demonstrates that localized inter-slice continuity can be effectively incorporated into 2D CAC segmentation frameworks without full volumetric processing. The findings support technical feasibility in the evaluated cohort, while external validation and assessment of downstream calcium scoring are needed before clinical application.
